question: 757. Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the progress made on coronial reform, including the preparation of Heads of Bill; his plans to establish formal agreements between his Department, the HSE, and coroners to ensure sustainable provision of medicolegal autopsies and prevent further service cessations in hospitals; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [7476/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration Coroners are independent office holders, and my Department has no role in directing their work during their investigation of any death. Neither does my Department have any role in relation to the work of pathologists who, as clinicians, undertake postmortem examinations on the direction of a coroner. Policy and operational responsibilities for the provision of postmortem examination services to support the work of the Coroner Service are supported by several departments and agencies. My Department is responsible for the legislation underpinning the work of coroners, while the provision of the postmortem examination service is largely provided through the Health Service and its personnel. Pathologists, other than forensic pathologists in the Office of the State Pathologist, are not contracted to either my Department, or to coroners. Where a postmortem examination is deemed to be required, the coroner will arrange for it to be conducted as expeditiously as possible in order to ensure the timely release of remains to the next of kin of the deceased. Depending on the circumstances of the death, a postmortem examination may be deemed necessary by the coroner, and is carried out by a pathologist or, in forensic cases, by the Office of the State Pathologist. A coroner’s investigation into a death may be finalised upon receipt of the postmortem examination report. In 2022, my Department established a ‘Standing Committee on the Provision of Coroner Directed postmortem examination services', membership of which is drawn from my Department, other relevant Government Departments, including the Department of Health, the Health Service Executive, the Office of the State Pathologist, An Garda Síochána, the Coroners Society of Ireland, and the Faculty of Pathology, Royal College of Physicians Ireland. Securing the provision of the postmortem examination service for the coronial death investigation function is challenging and I have been engaging with the Minister for Health to address this. There are issues arising within the pathology profession generally, including relating to training and recruitment, as well as competing demands on pathologists in areas of diagnostic and research work. I acknowledge those concerns. However, a long-term sustainable solution is nevertheless required, whereby this important service to the community is provided from within the pathology profession in Ireland generally. In October 2024, Government approval was given to draft a general scheme of a Bill to significantly reform the Coroner Service. As part of this work, my Department is examining ways to increase efficiencies and minimise the impact of the death investigation process on bereaved people. Department officials are currently working on drafting Heads of Bill in this regard, with the aim of bringing this before Government in the coming months. The proposed legislation to reform the Coroner Service will provide for a national coronial service to be centrally funded, thereby removing the responsibility for coronial services outside of the Dublin area from the local authorities. It will also provide for the establishment of an independent Office of the Chief Coroner, full-time salaried coroners and discontinue the existing fee-based system. A restructured and modernised Coroner Service will drive consistency and will assist coroners to better meet the needs of bereaved people, through the provision of enhanced ICT, administrative and family liaison supports.

question: 758. Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if his attention has been drawn to the visa application by a family (details supplied); if the specific circumstances can be taken into consideration as the process progresses; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [7587/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice I propose to take Questions Nos. 758 and 759 together. I can advise the Deputy that the Join Family (Non-EEA nat.)(other) visa application referred to was created on 13 December 2025. Supporting documentation was received in the New Delhi Visa Office on 19 December 2025 where it awaits examination and processing. I am acutely aware that join family applications are very important for those impacted and I understand that people are eager to have their families join them in Ireland. My Department's business target for join family visa applications is 12 months. It must be made clear that this is a business target for the immigration service and some applications can take longer than others. While processing times can vary across the different Visa Offices and Irish Embassies, the majority of visas are processed within stated target times. However, some applications can take considerably longer. Processing times for all applications are influenced by a number of factors. The time it can take varies depending on the type and complexity of application; individual circumstances; peak application periods; such as holidays or the start of the school year; and, crucially, the quality and completeness of the application lodged. Verifying an application is an important part of our immigration system and the checks involved can take time to complete. Processing times and decisions at the Dublin Visa Office and the Overseas Visa Offices can be checked at the following link: www.irishimmigration.ie/visa-decisions/ . While I acknowledge the personal difficulties an applicant might be experiencing; it is not possible to give a definitive date as to when this application will be finalised. All applications are processed in chronological order, based on date of receipt. I can further advise the Deputy that requests to expedite an application or for an emergency visa can be made through my Department's Customer Service Portal. Applicants can also use this portal to check the status of their visa application by registering for, or logging into, their account, at: www.portal.irishimmigration.ie/en/ . Expediting a visa application is usually confined to time-sensitive instances, such as, if a family member has been hospitalised, in a life-threatening situation, or in the unfortunate event of a bereavement. Each request is considered on its merits; the person concerned should also engage with the relevant Embassy of Ireland, explaining the nature of the emergency and provide any documentary evidence that may be available to them. A full list of Irish embassies is available at the following link: www.ireland.ie/en/dfa/embassies/ . Emergency visa applications and requests are dealt with on a case-by-case basis and are, where possible, processed as speedily and sympathetically as circumstances allow. However, in order to be fair to all those who have applied, not all requests to expedite an application can be granted. I understand that extended wait times can be frustrating for applicants, and I want to assure anyone who has made an application for a visa that my Department is doing everything possible to progress these applications as quickly as possible. As an Oireachtas member, you can also request the status of individual immigration cases by e-mail, using the Oireachtas Mail facility at: IMoireachtasmail@justice.ie, which has been specifically established for this purpose. This service enables up to date information on such cases to be obtained without the need to seek information by way of the Parliamentary Question process.

question: 760. Deputy Matt Carthy asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if he plans to designate a unit within An Garda Síochána to act as the verifying authority in the State for the purpose of Article 6 of the Eurodac Regulation; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [7619/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The International Protection Bill 2026 provides that the Minister may by order designate a unit within An Garda Síochána to be the verifying authority in the State for the purpose of Article 6 of the Eurodac Regulation. The Bill also provides for proper separation, as required by the Eurodac Regulation, between the unit within An Garda Síochána that is to act as verifying authority and the unit that is to act as designated authority for the purposes of Article 5 of the Eurodac Regulation. While the Minister plans to make such a designation following the enactment of the Bill, the exact unit that will be designated will be a matter for further discussion between the Minister and the Commissioner of An Garda Síochána, in view of the latter’s responsibility for operational matters.

question: 762. Deputy Matt Carthy asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the qualification or language competencies a cultural mediator will be required to have under the International Protection Bill 2026; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [7622/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I can assure the Deputy that I am fully committed to ensuring that Ireland’s International Protection system is robust and rules based, and that our borders are protected. As part of this, my Department ensures that international protection applications are dealt with fairly and efficiently within the framework of Ireland's international obligations. The International Protection Office (IPO) primarily provides cultural mediators through a partnership with the UN’s International Organisation for Migration (IOM). The role of the cultural mediator is to independently assist and support the applicant in the international protection process in the language of their choice. All cultural mediators employed are subject to both an IPO and separate IOM Code of Conduct. The International Bill defines the role of cultural mediators in broad terms and provides that I as Minister can make arrangements to allow cultural mediators to assist the applicant during the screening process, including the provision of information and support to the applicant. I am satisfied that this makes adequate provision for the role of cultural mediators in the process and that the terms of these services can continue to be provided for by way of the contractual arrangements in place between the Department and IOM.

question: 764. question: 765. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration whether he intends to review existing fraud and sentencing legislation to ensure penalties for deliberate insurance fraud appropriately reflect the seriousness of the offence and its impact on insurance costs and public confidence in the justice system. [7658/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration This Government recognises that insurance fraud is one of several factors that contribute to the cost of insurance. My Department is actively contributing to a programme of insurance reform which is being implemented on a whole-of-government basis. In relation to existing legislation, section 6 of the Criminal Justice (Theft and Fraud Offences) Act 2001 provides that "a person who dishonestly, with the intention of making a gain for himself or herself or another, or of causing loss to another, by any deception induces another to do or refrain from doing an act is guilty of an offence". A person guilty of the offence is liable on conviction on indictment to a fine or imprisonment for a term not exceeding 5 years or both. Further to this, the Criminal Justice (Perjury and Related Offences) Act 2021 was signed into law in June 2021, representing another tool to help tackle fraud. This places perjury on a criminal footing for the first time, thereby making the offence easier to prosecute. The Act increases the range of options for investigation, prosecution and the penalties on conviction which can be considered for those making false and misleading claims.

question: 773. Deputy Ruth Coppinger asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the criteria used to select EU nationals who were recently deported under the Free Movement Directive; if any of those deported had Irish citizen spouses or children; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [7706/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The removal of people who are involved in criminality and those who are a danger to society is a priority for me as Minister and my Department works closely with An Garda Síochána and the Irish Prison Service to ensure high risk persons are prioritised for removal from Ireland. Under the European Communities (Free Movement of Persons) Regulations 2015, which transposes the Free Movement Directive (Directive 2004/38/EC) into Irish law, orders can be made for both the removal and exclusion of citizens of the European Union, European Economic Area and Switzerland. Such orders are made after a full assessment of a person’s individual circumstances and can be made on the grounds of public policy, public security or public health; legally, such orders must not be disproportionate and an individual assessment of factors such as length of residence in the country, integration (e.g. work history), age, health etc. must be carried out. As the Deputy will be aware, on Sunday 25 January 2026, removal orders were enforced against 17 Polish citizens and 16 Lithuanian citizens who were removed from Ireland by charter flight. This was the State's second charter EU removal flight since the recommencement of charter flights last year, and followed an operation in October 2025 to remove 23 Romanian citizens. These removal orders were made in accordance with the Free Movement Directive on grounds of criminality and re-entry bans of up to 10 years have been applied to prevent return to Ireland. None of the individuals removed advanced any evidence to indicate that they were the spouse of an Irish national. Information in relation to 7 children (related to 7 of the individuals who were removed) was provided; two of which are confirmed to be have been born in Ireland. No evidence in relation to the nationality of the other 5 children was advanced.

question: 774. Deputy Joe Neville asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if his attention has been drawn to the unacceptable use of bunk beds in an IPAS centre (details supplied); if his attention has been drawn to an official inspection report dated 13 May 2025 that management at the centre attributed responsibility for this shortcoming to the contracting Department at that time; whether he regards such non-compliance with standards, along with associated overcrowding and inadequate wash basin and toilet facilities (as also raised in the same inspection report), as being serious breaches of State contract requirements; whether such non-compliance will be fully taken into account when the contract in question becomes due for renewal; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [7726/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 774 and 775 together. The State is currently accommodating over 33,000 people seeking international protection in over 312 International Protection Accommodation Service (IPAS) centres around the country. My Department has held a contract with a provider at Ryevale House since 2023 for the provision of international protection accommodation. Ryevale House was originally contracted to provided accommodation to up to 92 single female residents across 17 rooms, and met the standards required in terms of space, fire safety and insurance documentation. The use of bunk beds can be a feature of some IPAS Accommodation Centres, particularly since 2022 when severe shortages of available accommodation came into focus. IPAS notes the use of bunkbeds increases capacity within the accommodation portfolio. Due to urgent need for accommodation, use of bunkbeds is considered necessary and proportionate. However, steps have been taken to minimise the use of bunkbeds where possible. In relation to the need to have the water supply at Ryevale House augmented by tanker deliveries, the Department has been aware of this requirement since 2023, and that the provider was responsible for the arrangement of this service. The Department became aware of concerns about the source of the water being provided to the property through the media in 2025. The Department immediately sought an update from the provider. The provider, on foot of these reports, changed the supplier of water to the site. In relation to potential enforcement actions relating to the sourcing of water, apart from elements of the terms of our contract at this property, these are not within the remit of our Department to progress, and our understanding is that this would be the prerogative of the Local Authority. Significant work has been done in the last year to address existing compliance matters at IPAS centres nationwide, and to update and improve processes across the entire system. This work is proving effective, and will be ongoing into 2026 and beyond. I am not able to give details of ongoing contractual discussions at a specific centre, as they are treated as confidential while they are ongoing. However, the direction of travel for the IPAS system is to achieve improved value for money, to increase State-owned provision by moving away from reliance on commercial providers, and to continue to improve governance and compliance.

question: 776. Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration his views on the merits of creating a support service to assist jurors who have been on a jury for a distressing trial; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [7746/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration My Department has been advised by the Courts Service that they are mindful of the need to appreciate and support jurors both during and after criminal trials. To that end, there have been significant improvements to the jury experience in recent years. This includes the introduction of a digitalised jury summons and response process via an online jury portal, which is also an accessible and easy way for jurors to learn about the trial process and what to expect. The Courts Service is currently piloting a juror “Thank You” card which includes a link to HSE provided information and advice about mental health and wellbeing. The Courts Service has also invested in the provision of improved jury facilities in modernised courthouses across the country, which take into account privacy, security and refreshment needs for jurors. My Department is currently undertaking a review of jury service. This review is informed by research on the topic including the Law Reform Commission’s Report on Jury Service and legislative and policy developments in related areas over the past number of years. For this review, my Department engaged in a targeted consultation process with stakeholders and voluntary sectors. Responses to this consultation have been received and are being considered. The Department will consider its next steps in progressing the review, including whether further engagement is needed.

question: 777. Deputy Ann Graves asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration for an update on the redress scheme for the Stardust survivors; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [7747/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration Following the state apology and engagement with legal representatives of the families of the victims of the Stardust fire, the Government, in August 2024, approved a two-phased approach to redress arrangements. Phase one of the redress involved the establishment of a €24 million ex gratia redress scheme for the families of the 48 victims of the fire. This has now concluded, with payments made to all the families that were affected. In line with the Government's 2024 decision, work to develop phase two proposals, concerning survivors injured in the fire, continues to be advanced by my Department. This assessment will, in developing an appropriate mechanism, consider the compensation awards made by the Stardust Victims’ Compensation Tribunal established in 1985. In preparing proposals for my consideration and for approval by Government, the guiding principles that informed Phase One are just as important for Phase Two. Given the passage of time, it is of the utmost importance that in developing an approach, we prevent further trauma for applicants and minimise any possibility of re-traumatisation. The process should not place a significant burden of proof on survivors and it is my intention that, when finalised, the process will be simple, non-adversarial and accessible without legal assistance. This assessment is at an advanced stage and I look forward to bringing proposals to Government for consideration, following which my Department will make the necessary arrangements for implementation, which will include the provision of additional information, including timelines, for survivors on this important matter.

question: 779. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the procedures which are in place within the Irish Prison Service to ensure compliance with GDPR principles of data minimisation and purpose limitation when communicating with staff; whether any data-protection breach assessments have been undertaken in relation to bulk email communications involving private email addresses; and if he will provide details of any guidance issued to IPS management on this matter. [7784/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 779, 780 and 781 together. I am advised by the Irish Prison Service (IPS) that it operates a comprehensive data-protection governance framework, including formal procedures for the reporting, assessment and notification of personal data breaches in accordance with the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and the Data Protection Act 2018. The IPS maintains a central Data Breach Log, overseen by their Data Protection Officer (DPO), which records all reported incidents, the associated risk assessments, and the rationale for any decision to notify or not notify the Data Protection Commission (DPC). In line with Article 33 GDPR, any breach assessed as likely to result in a risk to the rights and freedoms of individuals is notified to the DPC within 72 hours. Where a high risk is identified, affected individuals are also notified without undue delay. Compliance with these obligations is assured through mandatory internal reporting procedures, centralised assessment by the DPO, ongoing audit and oversight, and regular reporting to senior management and to the Department of Justice; Home Affairs and Migration. In the past three years, the IPS has notified the DPC of five personal data breaches, one of which related to internal staff communications. All reported incidents were assessed by the DPO in accordance with Article 33 GDPR, and notifications were made where the threshold for reporting was met. In the case of the internal-communications incident, the email was promptly retrieved and deleted, the staff concerned were reminded of their data-protection and confidentiality obligations, and a formal risk assessment was completed by the DPO. The DPC was notified following that assessment, notwithstanding the mitigating actions taken, in the interests of regulatory transparency. I am advised by the IPS that during the Covid-19 pandemic, the IPS Contact Tracing Guidance and the Covid-19 Contact Tracing Privacy Notice, both issued to staff, make clear that contact details collected specifically for Covid-19 contact tracing were to be used solely for that purpose. Contact details collected specifically for Covid-19 contact tracing were maintained separately from HR communication datasets, were accessible only to designated personnel for public-health purposes, and were not used for wider HR communications. The IPS has no record of any deviation from these controls. I am advised that there is no record of Covid-19 contact-tracing contact details being repurposed for wider HR communications. One isolated incident was identified in which a contact number originally provided for Covid-19 contact-tracing purposes was used in error on a single occasion for an alternative purpose. This was assessed by the DPO as low-risk, limited in scope and not systemic in nature, and it did not meet the threshold for notification to the DPC under Article 33 GDPR. More broadly, all reported incidents within the IPS are subject to initial assessment by the DPO, and notifications to the DPC are made where the statutory threshold is met. In the past three years, one such notification related specifically to internal staff communications. The IPS operates a robust assurance framework to support compliance with data-protection legislation. All staff receive an annual Confidentiality and Privacy Legal Obligations Notice outlining their statutory responsibilities under GDPR, the Data Protection Acts, the Official Secrets Act, the Prisons Act and Prison Rules, and the Civil Service Code of Standards and Behaviour. Staff are required to complete mandatory data-protection training, with refresher training monitored by the DPO. ICT systems are subject to ongoing monitoring and audit, including regular review of access logs and usage records. These measures ensure that staff access personal data only where necessary and lawful, and that any suspected breach is promptly identified, assessed and addressed. In summary, I am advised that the IPS has clear policies, procedures and oversight mechanisms in place to ensure compliance with GDPR, including strict controls on the use of personal data collected for Covid-19 contact tracing and a structured process for assessing and notifying personal data breaches.

Contact details collected specifically for Covid-19 contact tracing were maintained separately from HR communication datasets, were accessible only to designated personnel for public-health purposes, and were not used for wider HR communications. The IPS has no record of any deviation from these controls. I am advised that there is no record of Covid-19 contact-tracing contact details being repurposed for wider HR communications. One isolated incident was identified in which a contact number originally provided for Covid-19 contact-tracing purposes was used in error on a single occasion for an alternative purpose. This was assessed by the DPO as low-risk, limited in scope and not systemic in nature, and it did not meet the threshold for notification to the DPC under Article 33 GDPR. More broadly, all reported incidents within the IPS are subject to initial assessment by the DPO, and notifications to the DPC are made where the statutory threshold is met. In the past three years, one such notification related specifically to internal staff communications. The IPS operates a robust assurance framework to support compliance with data-protection legislation. All staff receive an annual Confidentiality and Privacy Legal Obligations Notice outlining their statutory responsibilities under GDPR, the Data Protection Acts, the Official Secrets Act, the Prisons Act and Prison Rules, and the Civil Service Code of Standards and Behaviour. Staff are required to complete mandatory data-protection training, with refresher training monitored by the DPO. ICT systems are subject to ongoing monitoring and audit, including regular review of access logs and usage records. These measures ensure that staff access personal data only where necessary and lawful, and that any suspected breach is promptly identified, assessed and addressed. In summary, I am advised that the IPS has clear policies, procedures and oversight mechanisms in place to ensure compliance with GDPR, including strict controls on the use of personal data collected for Covid-19 contact tracing and a structured process for assessing and notifying personal data breaches.

question: 793. Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of Garda stations that have been closed since 2020; the criteria used for such closures; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [7842/26]

question: 794. Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the total funding allocated to community policing initiatives in 2025; the way this compares to 2024; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [7843/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration Community policing is at the heart of An Garda Síochána, and all Gardaí have a role to play in community policing in the course of carrying out their duties. Community policing is also fundamental to the Garda Operating Model. Community policing is delivered across the country and is supported by the Garda National Community Policing Unit within the Garda National Community Engagement Bureau. Under Section 72 of the Policing, Security and Community Safety 2024, the Garda Commissioner is the Accounting Officer for An Garda Síochána and is responsible for the Garda budget, including its allocation across the Garda organisation. I understand from the Garda authorities that the information requested is not readily available due to the manner in which budgets are structured and allocated within An Garda Síochána. question: 795. Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the steps his Department is taking to address the recruitment and retention challenges within An Garda Síochána; the targets set for increasing Garda numbers by the end of 2026; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [7844/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration Getting more Gardaí on our streets to prevent and detect crime remains my priority as Minister. The Programme for Government commits to examining a range of further measures to enable An Garda Síochána to recruit 5,000 members across the five year term of this Government. I am fully committed to ensuring that An Garda Síochána has the resources it needs, with Budget 2026 providing unprecedented funding of €2.74 billion to support recruitment, training and staffing. At the end of December 2025, the latest date for which figures are available, the total Garda workforce stood at over 18,200, which included 14,425 Gardaí, 3,505 Garda Staff, and 308 Reserves. Recruitment into An Garda Síochána is now gathering real momentum and interest in a career as a Garda remains high, with over 11,000 applications received last year across two recruitment campaigns. Overall, I am informed by the Garda authorities that just under 800 trainees entered the Garda College in 2025, the highest number since 2018. This demonstrates that there is a strong and sustained interest in a career as a Garda amongst the public and further recruitment competitions will be run to ensure that there is a steady pipeline of new recruits ready to enter the Garda College. The next group of Garda trainees are due to attest from the Garda College later this week. It is expected that there will be four intakes to the Garda College in 2026 and intake numbers will also be supported by ongoing capacity expansion works at the College. Significant measures have been made to boost recruitment and retention in recent years including by increasing the Garda trainee allowance to €354 per week; increasing the age of entry from 35 to 50; and raising the mandatory retirement age to 62. In the interest of transparency, information in relation to the allocation of Gardaí by Division, Station and rank, is publicly available and can be found at the following link: https://www.garda.ie/en/about-us/our-departments/human-resources-and-people-development/garda-hr-directorate/garda-strength-breakdown-2025/ The Deputy should select the most recent month and access the file titled “ Garda Members by Division District Station 2009 to the most recent date ” for a breakdown of total Garda numbers by Garda station going back to 2009. The Garda Commissioner is responsible for the distribution and stationing of Garda personnel throughout the State under Section 33 of the Policing, Security and Community Safety Act 2024.

question: 796. Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of reported incidents of burglaries, in each county for 2024 and 2025; the strategies implemented to combat these trends; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [7845/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The Central Statistics Office (CSO) publishes crime statistics, including Burglary and Related Offences. The requested statistics for the years 2003 to 2024 by Garda Division and Station can be found at the following link: https://data.cso.ie/table/CJQ01 All reported incidents of burglary are investigated by An Garda Síochána. I am advised that An Garda Síochána has had considerable success in reducing the prevalence of burglary through Operation Thor, which focuses on the prevention of burglaries and associated crimes, throughout Ireland, using strategies which are adapted for both rural and urban settings. In the 10 years since Operation Thor was introduced, burglary and related offences have declined overall. The level of residential burglary during the winter months, October to March, has fallen by 75% since the commencement of Operation Thor in 2015. An Garda Síochána launched the Winter Phase (2025/2026) of Operation Thor on 1 October 2025. Under Operation Thor, the Garda National Drugs and Organised Crime Bureau (GNDOCB) co-ordinates and supports Divisional resources actively targeting organised crime gangs and repeat offenders, particularly involved in rural burglaries and crimes, through enforcement activity based on intelligence and the latest burglary trends. Gardaí conduct high-visibility patrols and check-points at specific times of day in known ‘hot-spots’ to reduce the movement of burglars, gathering intelligence on known offenders and regularly communicating with those in the community about crime prevention measures. Operation Thor also aims to reduce burglaries by ensuring every burglary is appropriately investigated to the highest possible standard and by monitoring crime data for changes in trends of burglaries, associated crimes and detection rates.

question: 797. Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if he is considering introducing mandatory minimum sentences for repeat offenders involved in public order disturbances; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [7846/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The legislative context for public order offences is established primarily through the Criminal Justice (Public Order) Act 1994, amended through the Criminal Justice (Public Order) Act 2003 and the Criminal Justice (Public Order) Act 2011. These acts legislate for various types of public order offences and associated maximum sentences. The Judicial Council Act 2019 assigned responsibility for sentencing guidelines to the Judiciary, to ensure consistency, while protecting the principle of constitutional independence. The Judicial Council was established under the 2019 Act to achieve excellence in the performance of judicial functions, high standards of conduct among Judges, an independent Judiciary, and public confidence in the judiciary and in the administration of justice. The Judicial Council is independent in the performance of its functions under section 6 of the Act and it established the Sentencing Guidelines and Information Committee under section 23 of the Act, who are responsible for drafting and monitoring sentencing guidelines. The administration of justice is a judicial function under section 34 of Bunreacht na hÉireann. While the Oireachtas legislates to define crimes and maximum penalties, the application of sentences remains a function of the Judiciary. The Supreme Court ruled in Ellis v Minister for Justice and Equality 2019 that mandatory minimum sentencing targeting only a specific subset of people such as repeat offenders is unconstitutional, and as such is not under consideration.

question: 798. Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the current processing times for international protection applications from applicants originating from safe countries; the reforms planned to expedite these processes; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [7847/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration There has been a significant increase in investment into the international protection system which, combined with digitisation and process reengineering, has facilitated a major increase in processing capacity. In 2025, the International Protection Office (IPO) delivered over 20,200 first decisions compared to approximately 14,100 in 2024: a 44% increase. The International Protection Appeals Tribunal (IPAT) more than doubled the number of appeals closed from 3,100 in 2024 to nearly 6,300 in 2025. I can inform the Deputy that under section 72 of the International Protection Act, I, as Minister for Justice may make an order designating a country as a safe country of origin. A country may only be designated as a safe country of origin only if I am satisfied that, on the basis of the legal situation, the application of the law within a democratic system and the general political circumstances, it can be shown that there is no persecution and no real risk of serious harm. Ireland currently has fifteen countries designated as safe countries of origin: Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, North Macedonia, Georgia, Montenegro, Kosovo, Serbia, South Africa, Botswana, Algeria, Brazil, Egypt, India, Malawi and Morocco. Ireland has opted in to the EU Asylum and Migration Pact which will come into effect in June this year. The Pact will provide a fair, sustainable and efficient asylum procedure. This will be achieved through convergence in asylum practices across the EU, and through the introduction of streamlined and faster processing times. To prepare for its introduction, a phased transition that mirrors elements of the Pact is currently underway. As part of this, applicants from designated safe countries of origin, with some minor exceptions, are being processed under these new processes. As of January 8, there were 839 applications, and 623 decisions, with 541 or 87% being refused. These refusals have resulted in 190 Deportation Orders being signed, and 24 voluntary returns confirmed so far. The average processing time from when an application is lodged to a first-instance decision is 29 days. From application to appeal decision it is 50 days and from application to having a signed Deportation Order it is 59 days. This represents a significant shift from the current median processing times in the IPO and IPAT.

question: 799. Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the total number of deportation orders issued in 2025; the breakdown, by nationality; the enforcement mechanisms to ensure compliance; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [7848/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration It is a central priority for me that Ireland’s immigration system is robust and rules based. The enforcement aspects of our laws, including deportation orders, are an essential requirement for the system to work effectively and to ensure that there is confidence in the application of our legislation in this area. Deportations are costly and complex to enforce. It is the preferred option to return people voluntarily and my Department has a voluntary return programme to assist people to return prior to the issuance of a deportation order. A person can only avail of voluntary return before a deportation order is issued and I have increased resources into this programme to enable individuals who wish to return before a deportation order is issued to them. If a person does not remove themselves from the State following the issuance of a deportation order, they will be removed, and my Department has taken action to significantly improve immigration enforcement measures and increase removals. The number of deportation orders signed in 2024 (2,403) increased by 180% compared to 2023 (857). In 2025, 4,700 deportation orders were signed, an increase of 96% compared to 2024. In 2024, 1,122 people departed from the State under various mechanisms (i.e. enforced deportation, voluntary return etc.) In 2025, 2,111 people had their departure confirmed through these pathways, an increase of 88% compared to 2024. In 2025, six charter flight operations removed 205 people from the State. Of these, five operations to non-EU destinations removed 182 people who were subject to deportation orders and one operation removed 23 EU citizens on grounds of criminality. Table 1 below details the number of deportation orders signed in 2025 by nationality. Table 1. Deportation Orders signed 2025 by nationality Nationality Number of Deportation Orders signed Georgia 911 Algeria 542 Brazil 472 Nigeria 385 Pakistan 326 South Africa 197 Albania 192 India 170 Afghanistan 164 Egypt 154 Others 1187 Total 4700 * Please note, figures are correct at time of issue, however, all statistics may be subject to data cleansing. It is the policy of the Department not to release numbers where there are less than 5 in respect of any nationality as there is a fear that a person may be identifiable by releasing such information. Table 2 details the number of deportation orders enforced in 2025. Table 2. Deportation Enforcement 2025 Year 2025 Enforced Deportations 185 Removed by Charter 182 Otherwise Confirmed Deportation (1) 67 Total Deportations 434 Other Removals (2) 61 Number of Voluntary Returns 1,616 Total Removed 2,111 *Please note, figures are correct at time of issue, however, all statistics may be subject to data cleansing. 1. Otherwise confirmed deportations is where it has been confirmed a person has left the state following receipt of a deportation order without being escorted. 2. Other removals include Dublin III Transfer Orders of International Protection applicants to another EU State and EU Removal Orders for the return of EU Citizens under the Free Movement Regulations (these orders are made on grounds of criminality) and people who are deemed inadmissible under the International Protection Act. The enforcement of deportation orders is an operational matter for the Garda National Immigration Bureau (GNIB), and my Department works closely with the GNIB to progress arrangements for the removal of people subject to deportation orders. If a person issued with a deportation order does not leave the State independently then they are required to present to the GNIB in accordance with the conditions of their deportation order. Charter flights resumed in 2025 and provide an alternative to commercial flights and can be more appropriate in circumstances when a group of individuals are being removed to the same destination. Charter flights increase the options available to An Garda Síochána to effect removals and deportations. In January 2025, the nationwide transfer of immigration registration functions from An Garda Síochána to my Department completed the full civilianisation of the Garda administrative immigration functions. Prior to this transfer, over 100 Gardaí were assigned to immigration duties. The release of these Gardaí has enabled Garda management to focus resources more on enforcement and operational matters such as deportations and investigations. As there are no routine exit checks at Irish borders, it is not possible to accurately provide the number of people who are currently in Ireland subject to deportation orders. Since 2020 over 300 of the people subject to deportation orders have confirmed they have left the State independently. It should be noted that many will have left the State without informing the authorities. I am informed that the GNIB has reviewed a large sample of cases of people subject to deportation orders; their inquiries suggest a very significant number of these individuals have left the State.

question: 800. Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the annual cost to the State of providing legal aid to international protection applicants for the period 2020-2025; the oversight measures to prevent abuse of this system; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [7849/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The Legal Aid Board is the statutory body responsible for the provision of civil legal aid and advice to persons of modest means in the State, in accordance with the provisions of the Civil Legal Aid Act 1995 and the Civil Legal Aid Regulations 1996 to 2021. Section 3(3) of the 1995 Act provides that the Board shall, subject to the provisions of the Act, be independent in the exercise of its functions. However, to be of assistance to the Deputy I have had enquiries made with the Legal Aid Board and have been provided with the following information. Civil legal aid and advice is provided primarily through a network of law centres by solicitors employed by the Legal Aid Board. The Legal Aid Board also engages private solicitors and barristers to provide services in international protection cases. There are 34 full time and 3 part-time law centres and specialised units. Specific law centres in Dublin, Cork and Galway currently include an international protection speciality. The table below shows the total expenditure related to the provision of legal aid and advice in the area of international protection, excluding pay and operational costs. The expenditure shown covers costs associated with private solicitors contracted through the Legal Aid Board’s Solicitors Panel for International Protection Matters, as well as barristers retained from the International Protection Barristers Sub-Panel. It also includes other service-related costs, such as expert medical reports, translation services, and interpreters. Year Non-Pay Expenditure 2020 €1,243,907 2021 €988,873 2022 €2,067,130 2023 €4,130,236 2024 €5,698,396 2025 €6,590,222 I am informed by the Legal Aid Board that there are several oversight measures to prevent abuse of this system. The Legal Aid Board strictly operates in accordance with the provisions of the Civil Legal Aid Act 1995 together with the Civil Legal Aid Regulations 1996-2021. The Legal Aid Board operates under oversight and governance agreements with my Department which set performance, compliance, and accountability standards and to whom the Legal Aid Board is accountable and answerable with regard to its use of the Grant in Aid provided to it. question: 801. Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of failed asylum seekers who have remained in Ireland beyond their appeal periods in the past two years; the actions taken to address this issue; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [7850/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration My Department takes all necessary steps to manage the international protection process efficiently and effectively, while ensuring the integrity of those processes is maintained at all times. Both the International Protection Office (IPO) and the International Protection Appeals Tribunal (IPAT) are fully independent in deciding whether or not to grant international protection. Each application is examined individually on its own merits, in line with national and international asylum law. People who have been refused international protection and have exhausted the appeals avenues through the IPAT are entitled to submit a request to review their permission to remain where their circumstances have changed since their initial application. If successful, they will be granted permission to remain in Ireland. If the permission to remain review is refused the persons will have the option of voluntary return, which if not accepted will in the normal course lead to the making of a deportation order. It is the preferred option to return people voluntarily and the Department has a voluntary return programme to assist people to return prior to the issuance of a deportation order. A person can only avail of voluntary return before a deportation order is issued and I have increased resources into this programme to enable individuals who wish to return before a deportation order is issued to them. The table below details the number of voluntary returns for international protection applicants over the last two years. The total number of deportation orders signed in 2024 (2,403) increased by 180% compared to 2023 (857). In 2025, a total of 4,700 deportation orders were signed, an increase of 96% compared to 2024. question: 802. Deputy Michael Collins asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration his views on the appointment, procurement basis and ongoing payments in respect of services provided by a company at a location (details supplied); and if he will make a statement on the matter. [7881/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 802, 803, 804, 805, 806, 807, 808, 809 and 810 together. I can advise the Deputy that the company referred to in the details supplied were engaged by the State from June 2022 until August 2025 to provide a number of services at Citywest Hotel and Convention Centre. These services were for routine internal building repairs or works, including the provision, maintenance and repair of panelling, the provision of mobile charging stations and the repair and replacement of shower flooring. Following the purchase by the State of Citywest Hotel and Convention Centre in August 2025, the Department is no longer directly commissioning work from this supplier. From March 2022 onward, the State has been responding to the sudden and then increasing humanitarian need caused by the war in Ukraine. This included the use of Citywest as an important hub for receiving, screening, accommodating and supporting the arrival of Ukrainian people who were beneficiaries of EU temporary protection. The company was engaged in June 2022 via direct award, in view of the urgent requirement for services at the time. The company was chosen as it had previous experience in supplying services at the location. The Department relied on the applicable EU procurement Directive 2014/24 to negotiate directly without prior publication, which can be utilised in emergency situations. The Department is satisfied that the services provided by the company were in line with its registered business activities throughout the period it was engaged. A total of €4,893,721.81 was paid to the company by the State for the period from June 2022 to 23 August 2025. As outlined above, the Department no longer pays the company and as such there are no future annualised costs that apply. Since the State purchase of Citywest the accommodation service provider is responsible for the provision of all services on site. The service provider is carrying out a review of all existing services and a procurement plan is being developed. The provider is contractually obliged to ensure compliance with all procurement regulations for any new contracts.

question: 811. Deputy Michael Collins asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration whether, prior to the State's purchase of a property (details supplied) a formal value-for-money assessment was undertaken; whether that assessment distinguished between the capital cost of the building and the ongoing operational costs associated with its use, including catering, security, staffing, transport and facilities management; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [7892/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 811, 812 and 813 together. Cabinet approval for the State purchase of the Citywest Hotel and Convention Centre for international protection accommodation was secured last year, on 17 June 2025. The purchase of the site is a key part of the Government’s strategy to develop a stable and sustainable accommodation system for people seeking international protection. State-owned centres are part of the Government’s long-term plan to reduce the reliance on private accommodation providers, resulting in better value for money of public funds and a more efficient international protection system. The purchase was approved following an extensive due diligence process, including appropriate survey, legal review, and independent valuation, in line with the Government Infrastructure Guidelines. These guidelines set out the value for money guidelines for the evaluation, planning and management of public investment projects, including purchase or acquisitions of assets or shareholdings, in Ireland. The full purchase price for the Citywest centre (including VAT) was €148,253,530 which is in line with the Government decision of 17 June 2025. Compared to the costs of the previous leasing model, the savings to the State will pay back the purchase price within 4 years. This estimate is based on expenditure in 2024 under the previous leasing model for accommodation for people from Ukraine and international protection at this location. It also includes consideration of the ongoing running costs to the State of providing accommodation at the site after the purchase. The purchase model represents prudent financial sense for the State in this regard, while also delivering a permanent State asset. The purchase expenditure will form part of the 2025 Appropriation Account in due course which will be subject to audit by the Office of the Comptroller and Auditor General (C&AG).

question: 814. Deputy Naoise Ó Muirí asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of Gardaí assigned to County Mayo in each year since the introduction of the new Garda operating model; the number of new recruits allocated to Mayo in each of those years; the current total Garda strength in the county; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [7914/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 814 and 815 together. In the interest of transparency, An Garda Síochána publishes information in relation to the allocation of Gardaí nationally. This includes a breakdown of Gardaí assigned to Garda stations in the Mayo/Roscommon/Longford Division. I am advised that the Mayo Division was amalgamated with Roscommon/Longford Division under the new Operating Model in 2022. This information can be found at the following link: www.garda.ie/en/about-us/our-departments/human-resources-and-people-development/garda-hr-directorate/garda-strength-breakdown-2025/ The Deputy should select the most recently available date and then select the file titled ‘Garda Members by division district station to the most recent date" for a breakdown of Gardaí by Garda station going back to 2009. To find the information in relation to the allocation of Probationer Gardaí by Division and Station, The Deputy should access the file titled “Allocation of Probationer Gardaí by Division and Station 2015 to the most recent date” for a breakdown of total Probationer Garda numbers by Garda station going back to 2015. The Garda Commissioner is responsible for the management and administration of An Garda Síochána under Section 33 of the Policing, Security and Community Safety Act 2024, which includes the distribution and stationing of Garda personnel throughout the State. As Minister I have no direct role in decisions related to the Garda Operating Model, as these are operational policing matters under the Commissioner's remit. I remain committed to supporting An Garda Síochána and the Commissioner to ensure that they have the resources they need for their vital policing work.

question: 818. Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if he will consider supporting a proposal to amend the firearms permit/licence renewal process to enable it to become a process similar to that of the online passport renewal service; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [8036/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration Reform of the firearms licensing system has been under consideration for a number of years. Extensive consultation has been undertaken, and my Department holds meetings and engages with various firearms stakeholders on an ongoing basis. An Garda Síochána also meet with stakeholder organisations in respect of relevant matters. The Firearms Act, 1925-2023 and the Firearms (Firearm Certificates for Non-Residents) Act 2000 gives the authority for granting licences to Superintendents and Chief Superintendents of An Garda Síochána. When considering firearms licence applications, Chief Superintendents and Superintendents are considered 'persona designata' and cannot have their decision-making process fettered in any way. My Department is the competent authority for the import and export of firearms, the responsibility for all aspects regarding the licensing of firearms for possession resides with An Garda Síochána, including any technical or digital amendments to their licensing processing systems. I am advised that my officials regularly engage with An Garda Síochána to discuss issues pertinent to this area of work, however neither I, nor my Department have any role in the issuing of firearms certificates.

question: 819. Deputy Donna McGettigan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the way in which the national counter-radicalisation strategy is being adapted to address the evolving nature of ideological extremism, which can be rapidly propagated through digital algorithms and may exploit vulnerable individuals; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [8058/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The proliferation of harmful material online and the echo chamber effect which can be created by digital algorithms is a contemporary societal challenge which requires a whole of government, and indeed a societal response. There is an emerging trend being observed across the EU of young people in particular ‘self-radicalising’ on the internet through repeated exposure to and engagement with harmful and extreme material online. An Garda Síochána keeps such threats and trends relating to radicalisation, extremism and terrorism under constant and active review. Their role in respect of countering these threats is multi-faceted and is part of the wider whole-of-Government responsibility for addressing this complex issue. An Garda Síochána are continually engaged in the detection and prosecution of relevant criminal offences, as well as liaising with Europol and online platforms for the removal of harmful material online. This work is complemented by a community-based approach to policing which is important in engaging with and building relationships with communities potentially at risk of marginalisation or social exclusion, which can also be a risk factor for radicalisation. The EU Knowledge Hub on the Prevention of Radicalisation brings together practitioners, policymakers and researchers working on prevention across Europe. Experts and practitioners from my Department, An Garda Síochána, the Irish Prison Service, the Probation Service, other Government Departments and from civil society are active participants in the work of the Group, which aims to foster collaboration to address the challenges of radicalisation, emphasising an integrated, policy-driven approach and a whole-of-society perspective. The Department of Culture, Communications and Sport has primary responsibility for Online Safety. The Online Services and Media Regulation Act was introduced and Coimisiún na Meán established to regulate online media, including enforcing rules about how online services or platforms should deal with harmful and illegal content on their services. Working with stakeholders to tackle the use of recommender algorithms to protect children from harmful content is a commitment of the Programme for Government. Meaningfully addressing this issue requires a holistic approach not just by law enforcement agencies but by stakeholders across government and private industry. Coimisiún na Meán introduced and enforces a binding online safety code for video-sharing platforms, which set out obligations for online services to protect users from and tackle the availability of defined categories of harmful online content. Coimisiún na Meán is also key to the enforcement of the Digital Services Act (DSA) in Ireland. The DSA is EU-wide legislation which requires online services to take steps to make the internet safer for users by addressing harmful or illegal content on their sites. The Department of Culture, Communications and Sport also leads on implementation of the National Counter Disinformation Strategy. Key to this Strategy, insofar as countering the potential for radicalisation of individuals online is concerned, are the actions to improve the digital and media literacy of our citizens, including young people. Developing and utilising critical thinking is one of the primary inoculations against misinformation and disinformation.

question: 821. Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if the contract with a company (details supplied) for the provision of asylum accommodation will be extended in March 2026 in view of the fact that it has no planning permission and is subject to an enforcement order from Kildare County Council; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [8133/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration In relation to the property mentioned, my Department has held a contract with a provider at this location since 2023 for the provision of international protection accommodation. In the case of all contracted IPAS accommodation centres, all planning matters are between the Local Authority and the accommodation service provider. The provider remains responsible for all aspects of building regulatory matters, compliance and service provision at the property. While my Department is not directly involved in planning matters, it is aware that the planning for this site is the subject of court appeal proceedings at this time. Any action that is required as a result of those proceedings will be followed up once they are concluded. With respect to potential for contract renewals, the provision of accommodation for international protection applicants is demand-led, which remains high, and each premises is considered on a case-by-case basis to decide if the contract will be renewed as it approaches its end date. At potential renewal stage, consideration will be given to the current and projected demand for accommodation, the provider's performance under contract, and compliance with standards and legal obligations, including planning and building regulations. Details of individual contractual processes are treated as confidential and commercially sensitive while they are ongoing. Ireland has adopted and is now working to implement the EU Pact on Migration and Asylum in mid-2026. Reforming and speeding up processing of applications should also serve over time to reduce the scale of the demand for international protection accommodation. The Department is working to increase the amount of State-owned international protection accommodation and creating a more stable and sustainable accommodation system. As developing these more sustainable state-owned accommodation system options will take time, the commissioning of emergency commercial accommodation will continue to be a feature in the short to medium term.

question: 822. Deputy Matt Carthy asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if his Department has carried out an assessment as to whether the mobility framework associated with the EU-India Free Trade Agreement, upon which negotiations concluded on 27 January 2026, will form part of the trade proposal that the Commission will bring to the Council, and therefore be subject to qualified majority voting (details supplied); to outline the Government’s view of the proposal; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [8157/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 822 and 840 together. The ‘Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) between the European Union and the Republic of India on a Comprehensive Framework of Cooperation on Mobility’ is a non-legally binding text setting out broad principles concerning the mobility of highly skilled workers, seasonal workers, students and researchers within existing EU migration rules. The text is clear that the MoU does not create new legal obligations or rights under international or domestic law, and that it is without prejudice to EU Member States’ competence regarding mobility and migration. The MoU is a political declaration outlining potential areas of cooperation, and is largely based on the migration framework set out in several EU Directives concerning the entry and stay of workers, students and researchers, and seasonal workers. Under Protocol 21 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU), Ireland does not take part in EU measures in the area of freedom, security and justice, which includes migration, unless we choose to opt in. As Ireland has not opted into any of the relevant Directives, mobility in these categories remains entirely subject to domestic Irish immigration rules. The MoU itself is not a legal instrument and does not have a legal basis in the TFEU pillar of freedom, security and justice. Because of this, the question of opting in under Protocol 21 does not arise. In line with the procedure on non-legally binding instruments, the European Commission transmitted the text of the Memorandum to the Council of the European Union and secured authorisation for signature on behalf of the EU as a non-binding instrument. The MoU was signed at the EU-India Summit on 27 January 2026. The MoU is not part of the EU-India Free Trade Agreement but is complementary to it. It aims to foster research and innovation, address skill gaps and labour shortages, and promote economic growth through mobility of highly skilled people. In these respects, many sectors in Ireland benefit greatly from the contributions of Indian citizens. Our domestic immigration rules, including visas and residence permissions, and the employment permit system operated by the Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment will continue to provide a managed pathway for suitably qualified individuals where roles cannot be filled domestically or from the EEA/UK/Switzerland.

question: 826. Deputy Matt Carthy asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to list the measures under protocol 21 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, which Ireland opted out of in each year since the introduction of the protocol, to date in 2026, in tabular form; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [8237/26]

Protocol 21 provides that “Ireland shall not take part in the adoption by the Council of proposed measures pursuant to Title V of Part Three of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union.” As such, Ireland does not, as a rule, participate in the majority of Justice and Home Affairs related measures, unless we notify of our wish to opt-in. At the time of the negotiation of Protocol 21, Ireland made a Declaration (Declaration No. 56) which stated that we would participate to the maximum possible extent in JHA measures, and particularly in the field of police cooperation. In line with this commitment, our participation in measures which are subject to Protocol 21 is kept under constant review, in particular where an opt in under Article 3 was not previously utilised. The list of measures Ireland has opted-in pursuant to Protocol 21, as well as the list of measures that automatically apply to Ireland by virtue of our participation in certain elements of the Schengen acquis (i.e. in accordance with Council Decision 2002/192/EC) is available at the following link -https://assets.gov.ie/static/documents/09fe3ad4/EU_Justice_and_Home_Affairs_Measures_Subject_to_Protocol_21_in_which_Ireland_did_Opt-in.pdf. In May 2025 I published the findings of a Review of the operation of Protocol 21, which is available at the following link - www.gov.ie/en/department-of-justice-home-affairs-and-migration/publications/review-of-irelands-protocol-on-the-area-of-freedom-security-and-justice-2024/. The review was undertaken by my Department and informed by detailed statistical analysis of relevant legislation, internal and external consultations, and by a targeted consultation process with a range of key stakeholders. Appendix D of the review contained a list of significant JHA measures that Ireland had not yet opted in to. That list incorporates major EU legal instruments (Regulations and Directives) and International Agreements, but does not include Decisions and Implementing Regulations. As part of the continued oversight of the operation of Protocol 21, officials in my Department are reviewing this list with a view to updating it as required, and when this body of work is completed, the updated list will be published on gov.ie. In the interim, I can advise the Deputy that among the measures Ireland has opted into since Appendix D to the Protocol 21 Review was drafted include: • Regulation (EU) 2024/1348 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 14 May 2024 establishing a common procedure for international protection in the Union and repealing Directive 2013/32/EU • Regulation (EU) 2024/1351 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 14 May 2024 on asylum and migration management, amending Regulations (EU) 2021/1147 and (EU) 2021/1060 and repealing Regulation (EU) No 604/2013 • Regulation (EU) 2024/1350 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 14 May 2024 establishing a Union Resettlement and Humanitarian Admission Framework, and amending Regulation (EU) 2021/1147 • Directive (EU) 2024/1346 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 14 May 2024 laying down standards for the reception of applicants for international protection • Regulation (EU) 2024/1347 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 14 May 2024 on standards for the qualification of third-country nationals or stateless persons as beneficiaries of international protection, for a uniform status for refugees or for persons eligible for subsidiary protection and for the content of the protection granted, amending Council Directive 2003/109/EC and repealing Directive 2011/95/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council • Regulation (EU) 2024/1359 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 14 May 2024 addressing situations of crisis and force majeure in the field of migration and asylum and amending Regulation (EU) 2021/1147 • Regulation (EU) 2024/1358 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 14 May 2024 on the establishment of ‘Eurodac’ for the comparison of biometric data in order to effectively apply Regulations (EU) 2024/1351 and (EU) 2024/1350 of the European Parliament and of the Council and Council Directive 2001/55/EC and to identify illegally staying third-country nationals and stateless persons and on requests for the comparison with Eurodac data by Member States’ law enforcement authorities and Europol for law enforcement purposes, amending Regulations (EU) 2018/1240 and (EU) 2019/818 of the European Parliament and of the Council and repealing Regulation (EU) No 603/2013 of the European Parliament and of the Council All Protocol 21 opt-ins are of course subject to the approval of both houses of the Oireachtas, following a Government decision to seek their approval, and I can advise the Deputy that officials within my Department are currently working towards seeking approval to opt in under Article 4 of Protocol 21 to the following measures: • Directive (EU) 2024/1233 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 24 April 2024 on a single application procedure for a single permit for third-country nationals to reside and work in the territory of a Member State and on a common set of rights for third-country workers legally residing in a Member State (recast) • Council Regulation (EU) 2017/1939 of 12 October 2017 implementing enhanced cooperation on the establishment of the European Public Prosecutor’s Office (EPPO) • Directive 2014/41/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council of 3 April 2014 regarding the European Investigation Order in criminal matters • Regulation (EU) 2019/818 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 20 May 2019 on establishing a framework for interoperability between EU information systems in the field of police and judicial cooperation, asylum and migration • Regulation (EU) 2019/816 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 17 April 2019 establishing a centralised system for the identification of Member States holding conviction information on third-country nationals and stateless persons (ECRIS-TCN) to supplement the European Criminal Records Information System and amending Regulation (EU) 2018/1726 • Council Decision (EU) 2023/1076 of 1 June 2023 on the conclusion, on behalf of the European Union, of the Council of Europe Convention on preventing and combating violence against women and domestic violence with regard to matters related to judicial cooperation in criminal matters, asylum and non-refoulement • Directive (EU) 2017/541 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 15 March 2017 on combating terrorism and replacing Council Framework Decision 2002/475/JHA and amending Council Decision 2005/671/JHA.

question: 828. Deputy Paul Murphy asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration whether he agrees with the recommendation of report commissioned by him called An Assessment of the Efficacy of Bail Laws in Ireland which states that "the responsibility for the prosecution of offences should be removed from the Gardaí and all future Court proceedings should be conducted by legal professionals" (details supplied); his views on same; matter and if he will bring forward legislation to implement this recommendation. [8263/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The report completed by Mr Lorcan Staines SC ‘An Assessment of the Efficacy of Bail Laws in Ireland’ was published by my Department in November 2025. I would like to express my thanks to Lorcan Staines for his work in compiling this comprehensive report. This examination of our bail laws and subsequent proposals underlines the need for additional actions to be considered, to ensure the criminal justice system effectively mitigates against risks that may be associated with individuals on bail. A number of the recommendations are under active consideration, or already in the process of being implemented, across my Department. Regarding the report’s recommendation that the responsibility for the prosecution of offences should be removed from the Gardaí and all future Court proceedings should be conducted by legal professionals, this was previously recommended by the Commission on the Future of Policing in Ireland (CoFPI). It was accepted in principle by the Government, subject to a further evaluation of the implications, including resources. That subsequent evaluation, which was undertaken by a High-Level Review Group (HLRG), concluded that the CoFPI change was not appropriate and recommended instead, the implementation of what they termed the Reform Model. A Summary Prosecution Reform Steering Committee was then established, to drive forward the detailed design and implementation of the Reform Model. Under the Reform Model, the HLRG recommended that An Garda Síochána (AGS) retain responsibility for the conduct of prosecutions in court. The HLRG also recommended that the Director of Public Prosecutions (DPP) be supported in substantially enhancing quality assurance of the prosecution functions by AGS, in the name of the DPP. The work of the Steering Committee is ongoing and good progress has been made on the design and implementation of the new model.
